1.pericope_label: Doth not wisdom cry? and understanding put forth her voice?... O ye simple, understand wisdom: and, ye fools, be ye of an understanding heart

schools.summary: Delitzsch reads the opening as composition rather than topography — the author heaps up synonyms which touch one another without coming together — and defends the passage twice against Hitzig, who took the high places for a mountain summit and judged verse 2 an interpolation, and who rejected verses 4 to 12 as spurious. Ellicott supplies the cultural background, setting the secret allurements of vice under cover of night against the open invitation of wisdom, and distinguishing the two words of verse 4 as great men and men of inferior rank.

Gill takes Wisdom for Christ outright, arguing from the subsistence with the Father, the eternal existence, and the personal properties ascribed to her throughout; he hears in the crying a herald lifting his voice at noonday in the public street, against the whispers of a harlot at night in a corner, and reads the address of verse 4 as men indefinitely, of whatever rank.

Clarke refuses the christological reading sharply — wisdom is personified two ways only, as the power of judging rightly and as an attribute of God displayed in creation, whatever some of the fathers may have dreamed — and works the geography, suspecting that the constituted house of the paths means the house of public worship. But he will not leave it there: multitudes never enter such places, so wisdom must go out to them. On verse 5 he turns the text into a complaint about preaching that is not pointed. Wesley calls the identity of Wisdom a great question and declines to settle it.

Henry reads revelation as easy to come at, proclaimed aloud and from on high and where the crowds are; he notices independently of Gill that the adulterous woman spoke in secret and the heathen oracles muttered, while wisdom speaks openly, since truth seeks no corners but gladly appeals to the light.

debates.question: Who is Wisdom in this chapter?

positions.summary: Christ, the Wisdom of God — as appears from her subsistence with the Father, her eternal existence, and the personal properties and actions ascribed to her throughout.

Not a person at all: wisdom personified in two ways only, as the power of judging rightly and as an attribute of God displayed in the works of creation, and it has no other meaning in the whole chapter.

A great question that cannot be settled, since some passages agree better with the attribute and others with the person; possibly both are joined, and the chapter is to be read of Christ partly in his person and partly in his office.

debates.question: Who is being addressed in verse 4?

positions.summary: Men of wealth and power in the first word and the whole race of Adam in the second, so that the call runs from the greatest down to every individual.
Men indefinitely, of whatever rank, state or condition — all men without exception.

outliers.summary: Turns verse 5 into a complaint about preaching: teaching that does not specify vices and charge them home on the conscience never does much good, and the preacher who assures his hearers that these were the crimes of Jews and Greeks but he hopes better things of them arms their consciences in double brass against his own teaching.

Defends the integrity of the passage against Hitzig on two counts: the high places are not mountain summits, so verse 2 is no interpolation; and if the preamble of verses 4 to 12 is not to every taste, it still belongs by its circle of conception and thought.

themes: Doth not wisdom cry? and understanding put forth her voice?
She standeth in the top of high places, by the way in the places of the paths.
She crieth at the gates, at the entry of the city, at the coming in at the doors.
Unto you, O men, I call; and my voice is to the sons of man.
O ye simple, understand wisdom: and, ye fools, be ye of an understanding heart.

6.pericope_label: Hear; for I will speak of excellent things; and the opening of my lips shall be right things... For wisdom is better than rubies; and all the things that may be desired are not to be compared to it

schools.summary: Delitzsch reports the whole history of the word rendered excellent things — Hitzig's conspicuous, the Venice Greek's opposite, Kimchi's aim, and Fürst's derivation from a root meaning elevated and so visible, giving principal or pre-eminent — and resolves the apparent prohibition of silver in verse 10 by a rule of comparative negation, citing an Arabic saying built the same way. Ellicott corrects two words and grounds the plainness of verse 9 in the scriptural principle that the natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit.

Gill turns the promises into doctrine, hearing in verse 8 the necessity of righteousness and the worth of Christ's, and draws the sharpest form of the plainness of verse 9 — that the Bible is a sealed book to others, learned or unlearned alike — while conceding that the things necessary to salvation are easy. On verse 10 he insists that silver may be desired and received consistently with wisdom's instructions, and that what is forbidden is the immoderate pursuit.

Clarke glosses the excellent things as pre-eminent and manifestly superior, adding that the teaching is not trifling though addressed to triflers; renders the negative words of verse 8 as tortuous and as distorted, leading to obstinacy; takes righteousness in the legal sense of giving each his due; and makes the plainness of verse 9 conditional on self-knowledge. Wesley states the mind God has enlightened.

debates.question: What does the word rendered 'excellent things' mean?

positions.summary: Principal or pre-eminent things, from a root meaning to be elevated and therefore visible — the sense the Greek, Theodotion and Jerome all took.
Princely things, becoming to him who is Prince of the kings of the earth.

No — such negations are to be understood comparatively, so the sense is not do without silver but acquire wisdom instead of it, on the pattern of the old Arabic saying, the fire, and not the disgrace.

No — silver may be desired and received consistently with wisdom's instructions; what is forbidden is the anxious and immoderate pursuit that hinders their reception, and when the two compete the one is to be preferred.

outliers.summary: Presses the plainness of verse 9 into its hardest form: the Bible is a sealed book to others, learned or unlearned alike, and the mysteries are hidden in parables from them — though he adds that the things necessary to salvation are easily understood.

themes: Hear; for I will speak of excellent things; and the opening of my lips shall be right things.
For my mouth shall speak truth; and wickedness is an abomination to my lips.
All the words of my mouth are in righteousness; there is nothing froward or perverse in them.
They are all plain to him that understandeth, and right to them that find knowledge.
Receive my instruction, and not silver; and knowledge rather than choice gold.
For wisdom is better than rubies; and all the things that may be desired are not to be compared to it.

12.pericope_label: I wisdom dwell with prudence, and find out knowledge of witty inventions... By me princes rule, and nobles, even all the judges of the earth

schools.summary: Delitzsch renders the opening verb as inhabiting — wisdom has taken up residence in prudence, is at home in its whole sphere and rules it — marks a new series beginning at verse 13, and works the political vocabulary of verses 15 and 16: the verb means to decree rather than to legislate, the word for rulers comes from a root meaning weighty and so immovable, and the nobles are a fourth synonym for the exalted. Ellicott supplies the same verb and glosses witty inventions as well thought out plans.

Gill reads the first clause two ways at once, as prudence being the house Christ dwells in and prudence being his companion, and takes the whole section of Christ — the King of kings by whom kings are set up and to whom they are accountable. He is careful about which fear is meant in verse 13: not fear of judgment nor distrust of God's goodness nor a hypocritical show, but a filial fear consistent with strong faith and true courage.

Clarke calls prudence wisdom applied to practice, renders the witty inventions as knowledge and contrivance, draws from verse 13 the inference that hating evil and loving good are the sum of true religion, counts five degrees of civil power in verses 15 and 16, and notes that many manuscripts read judges of righteousness for judges of the earth. Wesley adds the qualification that a ruler's injustice is his own and only the good he does is owed to wisdom's conduct.

Henry identifies wisdom with Christ in the word and Christ in the heart, defines prudence against carnal policy, and claims that more witty inventions have been found by the help of scripture than were ever discovered by the learning of philosophers or the politics of statesmen — Christ himself having found the costliest of them, since we had found many inventions for our ruin and he found one for our recovery.

debates.question: What are the 'witty inventions' of verse 12?

positions.summary: Knowledge and contrivance — the power of combining what is known of the nature of things to produce new results.
Well thought out plans; ingenious contrivances for the glory of God and the good of men.
Discoveries made by the help of scripture, for understanding providences and countermining Satan's devices — of which the greatest is the salvation Christ contrived.

debates.question: In what sense do kings reign by wisdom?

positions.summary: By Christ, who sets them up and deposes them and to whom they are accountable, all the wisdom of their administrations being from him.
Only asymmetrically: their injustice is their own, and only the good they do is owed to wisdom's counsel.
Because all orders of government are from God, and the wise king is such through the influence of divine wisdom — five degrees of civil power being named here.

outliers.summary: Sets the inventions found by help of scripture against those of the philosophers and statesmen, and applies the verse to Christ: we had found out many inventions for our ruin, and he found out one for our recovery.

themes: I wisdom dwell with prudence, and find out knowledge of witty inventions.
The fear of the Lord is to hate evil: pride, and arrogancy, and the evil way, and the froward mouth, do I hate.
Counsel is mine, and sound wisdom: I am understanding; I have strength.
By me kings reign, and princes decree justice.
By me princes rule, and nobles, even all the judges of the earth.

17.pericope_label: I love them that love me; and those that seek me early shall find me... That I may cause those that love me to inherit substance; and I will fill their treasures

schools.summary: Delitzsch marks a fresh departure at verse 17, works the adjective of verse 18 from a verb meaning to move forwards — whence old, venerable, noble, and, of possessions, goods that increase and endure — and reads verse 20 as a claim about constancy, the verb form expressing firm continual action and the phrase in the midst meaning she turns aside on no side. Ellicott holds that the true riches are meant rather than material ones, and reduces the fruit and revenue to the gain that comes from possessing her.

Gill rules out both the incommunicable riches of Christ's person and temporal riches, leaving the riches of grace and glory; takes the fruit as the blessings of grace on the tree of life; turns the leading of verse 20 into a doctrine of justification, since Christ leads his people off their own righteousness first; and presses the word substance at its strongest, as what actually is, against the vain and shadowy things of this life.

Clarke traces the sequence by which love for wisdom arises at all — she shows a man himself, sets God's will before him, makes plain the snares of life — so that if the heart embraces the teaching, God's love is shed abroad in it and we love him because he first loved us. He grants that the wise man often does arrive at literal riches, then withdraws it, since this is not always so. Wesley takes the seeking early not of the hour but of the manner, with sincere affection and diligence.

positions.summary: Goods that increase and endure, as the Hebrew adjective itself implies.
Sometimes literal riches and honour, since the wise man often arrives at them — but not always, so what is chiefly in view is the durable riches, the treasure deposited by God in earthen vessels.
The true riches: not material wealth but the consciousness of God's favour, called elsewhere the unsearchable riches of Christ.
Neither the incommunicable riches of Christ's person nor temporal riches, which are not durable, but the riches of grace and of glory.
Not the hour but the manner: with sincere affection and diligence, which is the evidence that the love is real.
The seeking is answered by finding because wisdom repays love with love — this being the point at which her discourse takes a fresh departure.

outliers.summary: Takes the word rendered substance at its strongest, since it renders what actually is: the inheritance is not merely promised and laid up but already known, with the earnest of it in hand, and its solidity stands against the vain and shadowy things of this life.

themes: I love them that love me; and those that seek me early shall find me.
Riches and honour are with me; yea, durable riches and righteousness.
My fruit is better than gold, yea, than fine gold; and my revenue than choice silver.
I lead in the way of righteousness, in the midst of the paths of judgment:
That I may cause those that love me to inherit substance; and I will fill their treasures.

22.pericope_label: The Lord possessed me in the beginning of his way, before his works of old... while as yet he had not made the earth, nor the fields, nor the highest part of the dust of the world

schools.summary: Ellicott handles the disputed verb philologically rather than polemically: the Hebrew seems originally to have meant to set up or establish, and is used both of forming the heavens and of begetting a son, so that since set up and brought forth follow as synonyms, the earliest sense is likely intended — Wisdom formed or begotten before the creation, which agrees with the Septuagint. Delitzsch rejects both anointed and the woven or wrought of Hitzig and Ewald, preferring Aquila's I was appointed, and reads the depths as the inner waters and the settling of the mountains, with the Karaite Ahron ben Joseph, as into the bottom of the sea.

Gill traces the Arian use of the Greek rendering created me and answers on three grounds: the Word of God is nowhere said to be created; if he were, God must have been without his Wisdom before making him; and Christ as the Word is himself the Creator of all things. He insists the subject of verse 23 is a person and not a quality, and takes the begetting as the eternal generation, with the sequence before the mountains as a periphrasis of eternity showing the Son's eternity to be the Father's.

Clarke argues that wisdom is not acquired by the Divine Being but is eternally inherent in him as any other attribute, and calls the Targum and Syriac, which make wisdom a creature, as absurd and heretical as some modern glosses. On verse 23 he reads the verb as poured out or diffused, or from a cognate meaning to smear as with oil, and concludes that all the schemes of creation were conceived in the divine mind from eternity. Wesley glosses it as possession by eternal generation.

Henry argues from the grammar that an intelligent and divine person is speaking, not a mere property of the divine nature, since Wisdom is given personal properties and actions; and he concedes that Solomon himself may have designed only the praise of the attribute, answering that the Spirit who indited what he wrote carried him to expressions that could agree with no other than the Son.

debates.question: Does verse 22 say that Wisdom was created?

positions.summary: No: the Targum and Greek render it created me, and Arius built on that version, but the Word of God is nowhere said to be created, and the verb is better rendered begat me.
No: wisdom is not acquired by the Divine Being but eternally inherent in him, and the versions that make wisdom a creature are as absurd and heretical as some modern glosses on the same passage.

The verb originally meant to set up or establish, and since set up and brought forth follow as synonyms, the sense is that Wisdom was formed or begotten before the creation — which is what the Septuagint renders.

debates.question: Is the speaker a person or a divine attribute?

positions.summary: A person, since Wisdom here has personal properties and actions, which a mere essential property of the divine nature could not have; and that person can be no other than the Son.
An attribute: wisdom eternally inherent in God, as much as any other attribute of his nature.

outliers.summary: Draws from verse 23 the conclusion that all the schemes and plans relative to creation, government and providence were conceived in the divine mind from eternity, since there was no fortuitous creation, no jumbling concourse of original atoms.

themes: The Lord possessed me in the beginning of his way, before his works of old.
I was set up from everlasting, from the beginning, or ever the earth was.
When there were no depths, I was brought forth; when there were no fountains abounding with water.
Before the mountains were settled, before the hills was I brought forth:
While as yet he had not made the earth, nor the fields, nor the highest part of the dust of the world.

27.pericope_label: When he prepared the heavens, I was there: when he set a compass upon the face of the depth... rejoicing in the habitable part of his earth; and my delights were with the sons of men

schools.summary: Delitzsch takes the adverb of verse 27 as keeping its sense of place while including that of time — Wisdom was there when God created the world, having come into existence long before — rejects Hofmann's continually and the Targum's believing for the disputed word of verse 30, and reads the last verse as Wisdom turning her love to the earth for man's sake, and to man as a spiritual being whom she can bring back to God. Ellicott corrects established to made firm, prefers artificer to foster child, and notes that the pronoun in daily his delight is not in the Hebrew.

Gill insists the presence at creation was not a spectator's but a co-worker's, hears in the clouds waters bound up and yet not rent under the weight, reports that two Greek translators rendered the disputed word strengthened, and finds in the word for rejoicing something like sport or play, continuing the image of the nursed child.

Clarke turns each clause into physics — the compass on the deep as gravitation, the clouds as the ethereal regions, the sea's decree as the adjusting of its saltness and the proportioning of its surface to the vapour needed, the earth's foundations as the centrifugal and centripetal forces — and renders the word of verse 30 a nursling or darling child, warning that those who find the deity of Christ in these metaphors should be cautious lest in defending the truth they do something against it. Wesley reads the fountains as shut up in the earth's cavities, and makes the delight in men the whole work of redemption.

debates.question: What does the word rendered 'brought up with him' in verse 30 mean?

positions.summary: A nursling, a darling child — all the images of the verse being borrowed from a playful child near its parent.
A foster child in one sense, but more probably an artificer, which is much more suitable and better harmonised with the passages making Wisdom the agent of creation.
Strengthened, as two of the Greek translators render it.
Neither Hofmann's continually, for which the word is not so used, nor the Targum's believing or trusting, which is linguistically inadmissible.

debates.question: What is the compass set upon the face of the deep?

positions.summary: Possibly the establishment of gravitation, since particles tending to a common centre produce the orbicular form, so that even the waters take the circular figure in their aggregate of seas.
The stretching of the vault of heaven over it, or else the circle of the horizon.
The making of this lower world in the form of a globe, out of the abyss of water and earth mixed together.

outliers.summary: Warns against the reading most of the other commentators take: the language of verse 30 is poetical and highly figurative, and those who think they find the deity of Christ in these metaphors should be cautious how they apply such terms, lest while endeavouring to defend the truth they do something against it — in which, he thinks, most unhappily fail.

themes: When he prepared the heavens, I was there: when he set a compass upon the face of the depth:
When he established the clouds above: when he strengthened the fountains of the deep:
When he gave to the sea his decree, that the waters should not pass his commandment: when he appointed the foundations of the earth:
Then I was by him, as one brought up with him: and I was daily his delight, rejoicing always before him;
Rejoicing in the habitable part of his earth; and my delights were with the sons of men.

32.pericope_label: Now therefore hearken unto me, O ye children: for blessed are they that keep my ways... but he that sinneth against me wrongeth his own soul: all they that hate me love death

schools.summary: Delitzsch marks the hortatory close, notes that the Greek omits verse 33 and transposes the lines to remove an awkward conjunction, distinguishes the watching of verse 34 as a settled condition rather than wakefulness after interrupted sleep, and gives the verb of verse 36 its oldest sense of missing what one runs after or shoots at. Ellicott renders that verb he that misses me does not find me, and notes the Greek word for sin carries the same idea.

Gill fills in what missing means in practice — looking for salvation by the light of nature, the law of Moses, moral performances, or a bare profession — and ends the chapter where he began it, with finding Christ as finding life.

Clarke closes the chapter by refusing everything the christological reading has built on it: having weighed every word he cannot conscientiously reach another interpretation, the chapter speaks not one word of the divine or human nature of Christ, and had there not been a preconceived creed no one would have found the eternal sonship here by fair criticism. He states his own trinitarian belief nonetheless, and says the writers he opposes have taken away his Eternal Lord. Wesley makes the waiting that of servants at the doors of princes.

Henry states the design of the whole chapter from its close: to bring us into subjection to the laws of religion and make us wise and good, not to fill our heads with speculations or our tongues with disputes, but to rectify what is amiss in our hearts and lives — and so to read the word written, sit under the word preached, and bless God for both.

debates.question: Does this chapter teach the eternal sonship of Christ?

positions.summary: No. The chapter speaks not one word of either the divine or the human nature of Christ, much less of any eternal filiation of his divinity; had there not been a preconceived creed, no soul of man would have found the doctrine here by fair criticism — and the fathers, who are appealed to, were not agreed among themselves.
Yes: the speaker is Christ throughout, and finding him is finding life, spiritual and eternal.

debates.question: What is the force of 'he that sinneth against me'?

positions.summary: Missing rather than offending — the verb's oldest sense is to miss what one runs after, seeks or shoots at, and the contrast with him that finds me puts it beyond doubt.
Missing the mark by looking for salvation elsewhere: by the light of nature, the law of Moses, moral performances, or a bare profession.
Self-injury: it is not Satan nor sin properly speaking that hurts the man but himself, since if he received God's teaching sin would have no dominion over him.

outliers.summary: States his own creed while refusing the chapter's usual application — the holy Trinity, three persons in the Godhead of which none is before or after another, Jesus in his divine nature as unoriginated and eternal as Jehovah — and says of the writers who prove the eternal sonship from this chapter that they have taken away his Eternal Lord and he knows not where they have laid him.

themes: Now therefore hearken unto me, O ye children: for blessed are they that keep my ways.
Hear instruction, and be wise, and refuse it not.
Blessed is the man that heareth me, watching daily at my gates, waiting at the posts of my doors.
For whoso findeth me findeth life, and shall obtain favour of the Lord.
But he that sinneth against me wrongeth his own soul: all they that hate me love death.
